stories.title: A gift for every wedding moment
stories.dek: Weddings aren’t one day—they’re a string of moments, each with someone worth thanking. Here’s how to gift your way through all of them.

sections.heading: Start with the people standing beside you
sections.body: Bridesmaids and groomsmen show up for dress fittings, tastings, and the 6 a.m. hair appointment. A small, well-chosen gift when you ask them to stand with you sets the tone for everything that follows. Think a good candle, a silver bracelet, or a bottle of something bubbly—then make the reveal count with real wrapping and a handwritten line.

sections.heading: For the couple, give a reason to slow down
sections.body: The best couple gifts create time together after the confetti settles: a picnic kit, a proper coffee setup, a keepsake bouquet that never wilts. Registry gifts count too—a toaster becomes a celebration when it arrives wrapped like you meant it instead of in a brown shipping box.

sections.heading: Don’t forget the team behind the scenes
sections.body: Photographers, planners, florists, and the DJ who read the room perfectly all put in long, invisible hours. A thank-you gift—chocolates, a gift card, a bag of great beans—lands hardest when it’s unexpected. Send it the week after, when the adrenaline fades and gratitude is easy to miss.

sections.heading: Welcome out-of-town guests properly
sections.body: If friends flew in, a small welcome gift at the hotel says “we’re glad you’re here” before you even say hello. Local snacks, a water bottle, a hand-wrapped treat, and a card with the weekend schedule turn a hotel room into part of the celebration.

stories.tip: Shop the registry anywhere online, then add custom wrapping and optional flowers at checkout so the couple opens something beautiful—not a box inside a box.

stories.title: Make the first day feel like an occasion
stories.dek: Generic supplies do the job. The right gift, wrapped and waiting on the kitchen table, does something better—it turns nerves into excitement.

sections.heading: The one thing they carry every day
sections.body: A backpack is the most-used item of the whole school year, so it’s worth choosing well. For little ones, soft and small wins; for teens, something sturdy with room for a laptop. Add their name or a favorite summer photo and the “whose is this?” arguments end before they start.

sections.heading: Lunchboxes, bottles, and the small stuff
sections.body: There’s a quiet joy in opening a lunchbox that’s clearly yours. Pair it with an insulated bottle that keeps drinks cold through afternoon practice. These are inexpensive gifts that get used two hundred times a year—and they look far more special wrapped than tossed in a shopping bag.

sections.heading: For the student leaving home
sections.body: The first move to a dorm is a milestone hiding inside a chore. Send something that says “we’re proud of you”: a good laptop sleeve, a real coffee setup, a notebook for the ideas they’ll actually write down. Ship it wrapped so the first package in their new mailbox feels like home.

sections.heading: Teachers deserve a proper thank-you
sections.body: Thirty new faces every September is a lot. A small gift from a family—coffee, chocolates, a gift card—is a warm way to say “we see the work.” Wrap it properly and include a note from your kid; those are the ones that end up on the desk all year.

stories.tip: Order from any store, add Wrrapd at checkout, and the first-day gift shows up wrapped and ready—no late-night ribbon scramble.

stories.title: What to give the man who has everything
stories.dek: He already owns the gadget and the sweater. The trick isn’t finding something new—it’s finding something only you could have given.

sections.heading: Go sentimental, not expensive
sections.body: He doesn’t have the mug with your faces from that trip, or the glass etched with the year you met. Personal gifts sidestep “he already has one” entirely, because nobody else could have made this one. A photo book, a framed print, a puzzle from a favorite shot—these get kept.

sections.heading: Upgrade the everyday
sections.body: The gifts that win long-term are the ones he touches daily: a wallet that finally replaces the falling-apart one, a cutting board for his Sunday cooking, a bottle that keeps coffee hot on the commute. Useful beats novel—especially when it arrives looking like a gift, not a delivery.

sections.heading: When he says “nothing,” he means “nothing to store”
sections.body: Food and drink solve this instantly. Great coffee, a serious box of chocolates, a bottle of what he actually drinks—they get enjoyed, they disappear, and they’re always welcome. Pair a bottle with the right glass and you’ve built a complete, thoughtful gift in two clicks.

sections.heading: Or give him permission to indulge
sections.body: A robe he’d never buy himself, a proper barbecue tool set, a pair of headphones better than the ones he’s been nursing along. Luxury for men is usually just quality he won’t justify on his own—so justify it for him, and wrap it.

stories.tip: Whatever you pick, presentation does half the work. Custom wrapping plus a short note turns a practical gift into a memorable one.

stories.title: Cool gifts for someone who lives on coffee
stories.dek: Morning cup, after-school-pickup cup, after-dinner cup. Anyone this devoted deserves a gift that understands the ritual.

sections.heading: A mug for every mood
sections.body: You can never have too many mugs, but a real coffee person needs range: a tiny cup for espresso, a mid-size for a flat white, and one oversized mug for the milky weekend latte. A heat-reveal mug that shows a hidden photo when it fills is a guaranteed grin before the first sip.

sections.heading: Beans they’d never buy themselves
sections.body: Most coffee lovers stick to a house favorite. Gift the splurge: a roaster-direct bag, a seasonal blend, or a sampler of origins. It’s consumable, it smells incredible, and it arrives wrapped like something special instead of a grocery order.

sections.heading: Build them a coffee station
sections.body: Coasters that protect the good table, a serving tray for guests, a tin for the beans—small home accents that turn a kitchen corner into a café. Personal touches (a name, a photo, a favorite quote) make the whole setup feel like theirs.

sections.heading: The perfect pairing: chocolate
sections.body: Dark chocolate with a high cocoa percentage sings next to espresso; sea-salt caramel goes beautifully with a latte. Pair a bag of beans with a box of chocolates and you’ve made a gift they’ll think of you for, one sip and one square at a time.

stories.tip: Coffee travels well and wraps beautifully. Add flowers at checkout and it becomes a hostess gift, a thank-you, or a “just because.”

stories.title: Why an early thank-you beats a December gift
stories.dek: Everyone sends gifts the week before Christmas. The smartest companies—and the most thoughtful friends—send theirs at Thanksgiving.

sections.heading: Gratitude is the whole message
sections.body: Thanksgiving is literally about saying thanks, which makes it the most natural moment to recognize the clients, teammates, and partners who carried the year. Your gift doesn’t have to compete with a holiday theme—it just has to say “thank you,” clearly.

sections.heading: Arrive before the noise
sections.body: In December, even a beautiful gift gets lost between the office party, the school concert, and the dozen packages hitting the porch. Gifts that land in late November get opened, enjoyed, and remembered—because nothing else is arriving that day.

sections.heading: Better timing, better experience
sections.body: Carriers aren’t slammed yet, people are still home, and offices haven’t emptied for the break. A wrapped gift that shows up on time, before travel begins, is a gift that actually gets used—on the table, with family, over the long weekend.

sections.heading: Unexpected is unforgettable
sections.body: Because Thanksgiving gifting is still uncommon, it surprises people. Surprise reads as intention. Whether it’s a gourmet box for a client or a gift card and flowers for a neighbor, arriving first is often the most memorable thing you can do.

stories.tip: Send a few thank-yous now, wrapped and with a note, and you’ll have December to yourself.

stories.title: How to write a gift note they’ll actually keep
stories.dek: The wrapping gets the gasp. The note is what ends up in the drawer for years. Three lines are enough if they’re the right three.

sections.heading: Name the moment, not the object
sections.body: Skip “hope you like it.” Start with why now: “For your first week in the new place,” “Because you survived tax season,” “For the wedding weekend I’ll never forget.” Anchoring the gift to a moment makes it about them, not the thing.

sections.heading: One specific memory beats ten adjectives
sections.body: “You’re the best” fades. “You drove two hours in the rain to sit with me at the hospital” doesn’t. Pick one true, specific detail and write it plainly. It will land harder than anything a card company printed.

sections.heading: End with what you hope happens next
sections.body: A gift is a small wish for someone’s future: “May every morning start this well,” “Save me a seat at the first dinner party.” Close with that wish and sign your name the way you say it out loud.

stories.tip: Add your message at Wrrapd checkout and we’ll tuck it inside the wrapping, handwritten-style, so it’s the first thing they see.

stories.title: The holiday plan that saves your December
stories.dek: Nobody wants to be the person paying for overnight shipping on the 22nd. A little order now buys you a calm, generous month.

sections.heading: Make the list before the sales start
sections.body: Write down every name in one place first: family, the coworkers you always forget, your kid’s teacher, the neighbor who signs for your packages. Seeing the whole list at once shows where to spend properly and where a small, well-wrapped token is plenty — and it stops the December drift of three gifts for one person and none for four others.

sections.heading: Buy for the hard people first
sections.body: The person who “doesn’t need anything” is the one who will eat your last free weekend. Start there while you still have patience, while stock is deep, and while shipping windows are wide enough to fix a mistake. The easy names can wait until December without any real risk.

sections.heading: Batch the small gifts
sections.body: Teachers, sitters, mail carriers, the barista who knows your order: pick one good thing — chocolates, a bag of beans, a gift card — and buy it in quantity. The same gift, wrapped individually with a different note on each, reads as thoughtful rather than lazy, and it takes one decision instead of fifteen.

sections.heading: Hand off the wrapping
sections.body: The tape-and-scissors evening is the part nobody misses. Order what you like from any store, choose Wrrapd at checkout, and gifts arrive wrapped — including the ones shipping straight to somebody else’s house, which are usually the ones that would otherwise turn up in bare cardboard.

stories.tip: Ordering early also means you can add flowers to the December gifts that need to feel like an occasion rather than a delivery.

stories.title: Host and hostess gifts for the season of gathering
stories.dek: Somebody is cooking for twelve people and washing every dish afterward. Turn up with something better than the bottle you grabbed on the corner.

sections.heading: Bring something that outlasts the night
sections.body: A candle, a serving board, a good tin of olive oil, a set of coasters — things that stay in the kitchen long after the leftovers are gone. Hand it over wrapped and it reads as a gift rather than a contribution to the table, which is a surprisingly large difference.

sections.heading: Consumables are never wrong
sections.body: Chocolates, coffee, a bottle they’d actually pour. They add nothing to a house already full of things, and they usually get shared with the same people you spent the evening with. For a host who has been cooking for two days, something they can simply enjoy is the entire point.

sections.heading: Match the gift to the gathering
sections.body: A formal dinner and a chaotic family Thanksgiving want different things. For the first, something for the table or the bar cart. For the second, something for the host personally — a treat they can hide in a cupboard and open once the house is finally quiet.

sections.heading: Send it if you can’t be there
sections.body: When you can’t make the drive, a wrapped box with a real note lands harder than a text. Aim for the day before the gathering so it’s part of the table rather than a follow-up, and say plainly that you wish you were there.

stories.tip: Add flowers at checkout and the host gift doubles as the centerpiece—one delivery, one less errand for the person doing all the work.

stories.title: Teachers, coworkers, neighbors: the long list, handled
stories.dek: Twenty small gifts can feel like a chore or like the nicest thing you do all month. It mostly comes down to choosing once.

sections.heading: One good gift, repeated
sections.body: Pick a single item that suits almost anyone — a box of chocolates, a bag of beans, a gift card with a real amount on it — and buy it in quantity. Consistency isn’t laziness; it’s how caterers, hosts, and anyone who has ever run an office get through December.

sections.heading: Let the note do the personalizing
sections.body: The gift can repeat; the message shouldn’t. One line naming something specific — the late pickup they covered, the driveway they shoveled, the shift they swapped — turns an identical box into a personal one. Thirty seconds per person, and it’s the part they keep.

sections.heading: Set one number and stick to it
sections.body: Decide the per-person amount before you shop, not while you shop. A clear number keeps twenty small gifts from quietly becoming a car payment, and it removes the awkward arithmetic of whether the neighbor should get more than the teacher.

sections.heading: Presentation is the whole difference
sections.body: A wrapped box on a desk gets noticed; a plastic bag gets moved. This is where a small budget stretches furthest, because the reveal is the part people actually remember — and it’s the difference between giving a gift and handing something over.

stories.tip: Ordering a batch? Each one is wrapped individually, so twenty gifts still feel like twenty gifts instead of a bulk shipment.

stories.title: Gifts that keep the wonder going
stories.dek: Kids remember two things: what they opened, and how it felt to open it. Only one of those costs extra.

sections.heading: Build-together beats battery-powered
sections.body: A set they assemble with someone — bricks, a model, a baking kit — buys hours instead of minutes. The good ones come back out in February, which is the only test that matters. Needing an adult nearby is a feature, not a drawback.

sections.heading: Books age better than toys
sections.body: A book chosen for a specific kid, with their name and the year written inside the cover, stays on a shelf long after the plastic has gone. Pair one with something small and physical and you’ve built a gift with two acts instead of one.

sections.heading: One considered thing beats five cheap ones
sections.body: Five small gifts produce about five seconds of excitement each. One thing they’ve been circling since October produces a memory. If the budget is tight, spend it in a single place and wrap it properly rather than spreading it thin.

sections.heading: Make the unwrapping part of it
sections.body: Nobody photographs a shipping box. Real paper, ribbon, a name tag in actual handwriting — that’s the two minutes kids talk about later, and it’s the cheapest upgrade on the whole list. Wrap each piece separately even when it’s one set.

stories.tip: Shipping to cousins or grandkids? We wrap each parcel and include your note, so the box that arrives already looks like the morning itself.

stories.title: Gifts for the quiet weeks after the holidays
stories.dek: January is grey, everyone is broke, and nobody is expecting a parcel. That is precisely why one lands so well.

sections.heading: Make a cold morning better
sections.body: Great coffee, a heavy mug, a blanket that actually gets used on the sofa. Small comforts do more work in January than anything expensive did in December, because the novelty of the holidays is gone and the weather still has two months to run.

sections.heading: Support the new habit, gently
sections.body: Someone starting something — a class, a running routine, a new job — is easier to support than to surprise. Kit for the habit says “I noticed” without tipping over into pressure. Keep it light: the gear, not a lecture about sticking with it.

sections.heading: January birthdays deserve better
sections.body: Anyone born in the first three weeks of January has spent their whole life being folded into the holidays. A gift that clearly isn’t leftover Christmas — wrapped differently, sent on the actual day — quietly fixes a lifetime of mild injustice.

sections.heading: Send the belated thank-you
sections.body: Anyone who hosted, drove, cooked, or babysat in December was far too busy to be thanked properly at the time. A wrapped gift in the second week of January is unexpected, and unexpected is what people remember once the decorations are down.

stories.tip: A January gift with flowers is the cheapest way to make a dark week feel like an occasion.

stories.title: Comfort gifts for the coldest weeks
stories.dek: February asks very little of a gift. Warm, soft, or edible will cover it.

sections.heading: Warmth you can wear indoors
sections.body: Thick socks, a robe, slippers that won’t fall apart by March. These are the things people are faintly embarrassed to buy themselves and genuinely pleased to receive, which is close to a perfect description of a good gift.

sections.heading: A small luxury for the shelf
sections.body: A good hand cream, a bath set, a candle that smells like something other than “winter spice.” Inexpensive, used daily, and lovely when it arrives wrapped — the sort of thing that quietly improves February without needing an occasion attached.

sections.heading: Feed the hibernation
sections.body: Hot chocolate worth drinking, a tin of good biscuits, coffee for the long grey afternoons. Food gifts fit the season exactly: nobody wants another object in February, but everybody wants something warm at four o’clock.

sections.heading: Something to look forward to
sections.body: A book they mentioned once, a puzzle for a snowed-in Sunday, tickets to something in spring. Comfort isn’t only physical — sometimes it’s having a date on the calendar, which is the one thing February is genuinely short of.

stories.tip: Soft goods wrap beautifully. Add a note saying when to open it and you’ve made a small event out of an ordinary Tuesday.

stories.title: Valentine’s gifts that aren’t a last-minute bouquet
stories.dek: Flowers are lovely. Flowers grabbed at 6 p.m. on the 14th, still in the plastic sleeve, are a receipt. The fix takes about four minutes.

sections.heading: Pick the thing that references you two
sections.body: The record from the old apartment, the coffee from that trip, a glass engraved with a date nobody else would care about. Specific beats expensive every single time, because the gift is really just a way of saying you were paying attention.

sections.heading: Then make the delivery the romance
sections.body: Half of what people remember about Valentine’s is the reveal: how it looked, where it was waiting, what the note said. Wrapping isn’t decoration here — it’s most of the gift, and it’s the first thing a rushed evening sacrifices.

sections.heading: Keep the flowers, just plan them
sections.body: Ordered ahead and arriving with the gift, flowers stop being an apology and start being a flourish. Same flowers, completely different message. The only variable that matters is whether you chose them on Tuesday or panicked on Saturday.

sections.heading: If you’re far apart
sections.body: Send it to arrive on the 13th, not the 14th. A wrapped parcel waiting when they get home beats a video call with nothing to open, and it means the day starts well instead of hinging on the postal service.

stories.tip: Add flowers to any gift at Wrrapd checkout and the whole thing arrives together, wrapped, on the day you choose.

stories.title: Valentine’s for everyone else you love
stories.dek: Friends, kids, parents, the person who kept you sane last year. It’s a good excuse, and nobody said it was only for couples.

sections.heading: The friend who always shows up
sections.body: Chocolate, a candle, a small piece of jewelry, and a card that says the thing you’d never manage out loud. Low stakes, very high return — and February is one of the few months with no other excuse to send anything.

sections.heading: Kids love the ritual more than the gift
sections.body: A small wrapped box on the breakfast table on the 14th costs almost nothing and gets remembered for years. Books, stickers, one good chocolate — it’s the ceremony they’re after, not the contents. Set it out the night before.

sections.heading: Send one to a parent
sections.body: Nobody sends parents anything in February, which is exactly why it works. A wrapped box arriving with no occasion attached is the entire gift; what’s inside is almost incidental. Chocolates and a few honest lines will do it.

sections.heading: And one for yourself, honestly
sections.body: The bath set you keep not buying, the book that’s been in a browser tab since November. If you’re already placing an order for other people, adding a line for yourself is efficient rather than indulgent.

stories.tip: Ordering a few at once? Each is wrapped individually, so none of them feel like they came out of a batch.

stories.title: Easter baskets and spring gifts worth photographing
stories.dek: Somewhere between the chocolate rabbit and the plastic grass, the basket stopped feeling special. That’s an easy thing to fix.

sections.heading: Build around one real gift
sections.body: A book, a small building set, something for the garden — one thing that survives past Sunday afternoon. The candy is the confetti, not the gift. A basket with a single considered item beats one filled to the brim with foil wrappers.

sections.heading: Spring gifts for grown-ups too
sections.body: Seeds and tools for the person eyeing the back yard, a light scarf, good sunscreen for someone about to spend the summer outdoors. Spring gifting is mostly about anticipation: you’re handing over the season slightly before it arrives.

sections.heading: The first warm weekend deserves something
sections.body: Once the evenings stretch out, people start hosting again. A bottle for the first cookout, a citronella candle, a set of outdoor glasses — small things that mark the shift and then get used every weekend after.

sections.heading: Say thank you at the end of the school year
sections.body: Late spring is teacher-and-coach season, and everyone involved is running on empty. A wrapped gift in May, when nobody else has the energy left to organize one, is the gift that actually gets remembered.

stories.tip: Sending a basket to another house? Have it wrapped and delivered so it arrives looking like a gift instead of a grocery order.

stories.title: Housewarming gifts with staying power
stories.dek: Moving season runs from spring into late summer, and most people arrive at a new place with a great many boxes and no candles.

sections.heading: Give what nobody buys themselves
sections.body: Good towels, a serving board, a decent doormat, a wind chime for the porch. Practical things, one notch nicer than the version they’d have grabbed in a rush on moving weekend — that’s the whole trick with housewarming gifts.

sections.heading: Or give them the first night
sections.body: A bottle, a box of chocolates, coffee and mugs for the morning after the truck leaves. Consumables are perfect when someone has nowhere to put anything yet, and the first morning in a new kitchen is rough without coffee.

sections.heading: Skip the sixth candle
sections.body: If you know others are coming to the same housewarming, choose what nobody else thinks of: a plant, kitchen tools, a framed print of the new street. Wrapped well, that’s the one they end up mentioning to other people.

sections.heading: For a first apartment, think basics
sections.body: A first place is usually short on the boring things — a good knife, real towels, a lamp that isn’t the overhead light. Unglamorous gifts are enormously welcome when someone is eating dinner off a box.

stories.tip: Shipping straight to the new address? We wrap it and include your note, so the first delivery at the new place is a good one.

stories.title: Mother’s Day beyond flowers — but keep the flowers
stories.dek: She’ll tell you not to make a fuss. Make a small, well-organized fuss anyway.

sections.heading: Pick what she’d never justify
sections.body: The good hand cream, the nice earrings, the coat she looked at twice and put back. Mothers are famously bad at buying the slightly better version of anything, and that’s precisely the gap you’re filling. Buy the one she wouldn’t.

sections.heading: Or give her the afternoon
sections.body: A book and no plans, a brunch she doesn’t cook, a spa set and a locked bathroom door. The time is the gift; the object is just how you hand it over. Make the plan concrete or it quietly won’t happen.

sections.heading: Grandmothers, stepmothers, and the friend who mothered you
sections.body: The list is longer than one person. A small wrapped gift to someone who wasn’t expecting to be counted is the most surprising thing you’ll send in May — and usually the one that gets a phone call rather than a text.

sections.heading: Keep the flowers, add them properly
sections.body: Flowers arriving with a gift beat flowers arriving alone. Order once and have both turn up wrapped on the same morning, instead of juggling two deliveries and hoping the bouquet isn’t left in the sun on a doorstep.

stories.tip: Add flowers at checkout and we’ll deliver them with the gift—no second order, nothing wilting on a doorstep.

stories.title: Graduation gifts for the next chapter
stories.dek: Cards with cash in them are fine. Something they’ll still own in five years is better—and it doesn’t have to cost more.

sections.heading: Give what the next year needs
sections.body: A laptop bag that survives a commute, a real coffee setup for the first apartment, a good pen for someone about to start signing things. Useful, and a quiet vote of confidence in whatever they’re walking into next.

sections.heading: Make the money memorable
sections.body: If a gift card genuinely is the right answer — and for a graduate it often is — don’t hand it over in a bare envelope. Put it in a wrapped box with a note about what you watched them get through. Same amount, entirely different memory.

sections.heading: Mark the moment in something lasting
sections.body: A framed print, an engraved piece, a book inscribed with the date. Graduation gifts get kept far longer than most, so one small permanent detail — a name, a year, a line you actually mean — pays off for decades.

sections.heading: Don’t overthink high school
sections.body: For an eighteen-year-old, practical wins: headphones, a suitcase, something for the dorm. Save the sentimental keepsake for the people who already have somewhere to put it and a shelf to put it on.

stories.tip: Wrap it and write the note early—commencement week fills up fast, and the gift that arrives on time is the one opened with everyone watching.

stories.title: For the dad who says not to get him anything
stories.dek: He means it, and he’s also going to notice if nothing turns up. Here’s the way through.

sections.heading: Replace something worn out
sections.body: The wallet held together by habit, the grill set missing a tong, the headphones with the flaking earpad. Swapping a tired thing for a good version is the highest-percentage gift there is, because he’d never get round to it himself.

sections.heading: Feed him
sections.body: Steaks, a rub set, real coffee, a serious box of chocolate. Consumables sidestep the “I don’t need more stuff” objection entirely, and he’ll share them, which he’ll enjoy considerably more than the gift itself.

sections.heading: Lean into the hobby, not the stereotype
sections.body: If he fishes, the gift is tackle — not a novelty mug about fishing. Anyone with a hobby keeps a mental list of small upgrades they’ve been putting off; ask one question and you’ll usually get the whole list.

sections.heading: Give the day, not just the box
sections.body: The gift can be the excuse for a cookout, a fishing morning, a game together. Wrap the small thing that starts it and the day itself becomes the present — which is generally what he wanted and wouldn’t ask for.

stories.tip: The kids’ notes are the part dads keep. Add the message at checkout and we’ll tuck it inside the wrapping.

stories.title: Cookouts, cabins, and the summer gift calendar
stories.dek: Summer gifting isn’t one holiday. It’s a steady run of weekends where you turn up at somebody else’s house.

sections.heading: The cookout gift
sections.body: Not another bag of ice. Good tongs, a rub set, a cooler bag, a bottle for the host to open once everyone’s gone home. Aim for something that shows up again next weekend rather than getting consumed within the hour.

sections.heading: The lake house or cabin weekend
sections.body: When someone hands you a spare room for three nights, the thank-you should be planned rather than scavenged from a gas station on the way. Coffee for the mornings, a game for the rain, a candle for the room they cleared out.

sections.heading: Weddings, showers, and everything between
sections.body: Summer is peak celebration season. Keep two or three reliable gifts in mind — a home piece, a keepsake, a good gift card — so you’re never shopping at nine o’clock the night before with nothing good left.

sections.heading: Ship ahead when you’re travelling
sections.body: Nobody wants to fly with a wrapped box in a carry-on. Send it to the address you’re visiting so it’s waiting when you arrive: you turn up empty-handed and the gift is already on the porch.

stories.tip: Add your message at checkout and we’ll tuck it inside the wrapping — handy when the gift arrives at the house before you do.
